instruction: Fix this so it reads like something I would publish.
source_text: Our team is thrilled to announce that we have leveraged a cutting-edge observability platform to deliver world-class reliability improvements across the entire fleet. P99 latency was reduced by 40% and the error budget was preserved throughout the migration window.
why: The round-four failure: a rewrite that keeps the buzzword sitting in the middle of the sentence.

instruction: This is a voice memo transcript. Turn it into prose.
source_text: so yeah basically we kinda threw together a queue in front of the writes because the database was falling over every afternoon around two, and then like once that was in the write path got way faster, i think it was something like six seconds down to under one, and the takeaway is you should probably look at the write path before you buy a bigger box.
why: Dictation cleanup is one of the two jobs that survived. It has to keep the numbers and drop the filler.

instruction: Take the academic scaffolding off this and put a builder behind it.
source_text:
## The Hypothesis
It is hypothesized that developer onboarding friction is a function of unaddressed architectural constraints. 

## The Methodology
An empirical investigation was conducted across a representative sample of integration attempts in order to evaluate the veracity of this premise. It was determined that the authentication step accounts for the majority of abandonment events.
why: Rhetorical headings and agentless passive are the two tells I ask for by name.

instruction: Cut the rhetorical crutches out of this paragraph.
source_text: It is not about the tooling, it is about the culture. Our platform team spent the quarter building a golden path — which is mission-critical — and the results speak for themselves. Adoption doubled, because developers finally had a default that worked.
why: False antithesis, an em-dash, and 'the results speak for themselves' in one paragraph.

must_remove: re:it is not about .{2,40}, it is about

instruction: This is a LinkedIn post. Make it something a developer would not scroll past.
source_text: 🚀 Huge news! We are incredibly proud to unveil our next-generation AI Copilot, a truly transformative leap that empowers every engineer to unlock the full potential of their workflow. This is a game-changer for the industry. Massive shoutout to the whole team for making it happen! #AI #Innovation #FutureOfWork
why: The hype register. Nothing in the source is a fact, so the rewrite has to be short and cannot invent one.

instruction: Rewrite this incident summary so a reader can tell who did what.
source_text: An outage was experienced by customers in the us-east region for a period of 47 minutes. The root cause was determined to be a misconfigured connection pool. Remediation was performed and monitoring has been enhanced to prevent recurrence.
why: Agentless passive hiding ownership, which is the exact register I ban for my own work.

instruction: Compress this release note to the part a developer needs.
source_text: We are pleased to share that version 3.2 of the SDK is now generally available. This release includes a number of exciting enhancements and quality-of-life improvements that we believe will significantly improve the developer experience. Notably, the retry handler now supports exponential backoff with jitter, and the default timeout has been increased from 5 seconds to 30 seconds.
why: Two real facts buried under four sentences of throat-clearing.

instruction: Rewrite this so an actual engineer would apply.
source_text: We are seeking a passionate, self-motivated rockstar engineer to join our world-class team and take ownership of mission-critical initiatives in a fast-paced, dynamic environment. The ideal candidate is a strong communicator who thrives on ambiguity and wears many hats.
why: Job-posting slop, and every banned adjective in the lexicon at once.

instruction: Light pass. Fix what is actually wrong and leave the rest alone.
source_text: The gateway was dropping one request in every four hundred, and only under load. I found it by replaying a week of traffic against a single instance with the connection limit lowered to 50. The bug was a race between the health check and the pool warm-up, and it had been in production for eleven months.
why: The opposite failure. This is already fine, and an over-eager rewrite is a real cost when the model is a reviewer.

instruction: One thing in this violates my own style rules. Fix that and change nothing else.
source_text: I stopped writing the benchmark harness after the second week — the numbers I wanted were already in the request logs. Reading them cost an afternoon. Building the harness would have cost a month, and it would have measured a workload nobody runs.
why: A single em-dash in otherwise clean prose. Tests whether the model can make a surgical change.

instruction: Tighten this paragraph. It is close.
source_text: The migration took three weekends. The first one went to reading the schema, which nobody on the team had opened since 2021. The second went to the backfill, and the third went to the parts I had assumed would be easy. In order to avoid a repeat, I now read the schema first.
why: Only 'In order to' needs to go. A rewrite that touches the rest has failed.

instruction: Rewrite this in my register. Every number in it is real, so every number has to survive.
source_text: Utilization was made of a caching layer by the platform group, resulting in a reduction of origin requests by 62%, a decrease in p95 response time from 840ms to 310ms, and an annualized infrastructure saving of $48,000 across 14 services.
why: Fact preservation under a heavy register change, which is where a rewrite quietly drops a number.

instruction: Rewrite this so it sounds like me. Keep the link exactly as it is.
source_text: It has been demonstrated by researchers that fine-tuning on an author's complete works produces stylistic fidelity that prompting does not achieve. The preregistered study is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13939 for those who wish to review the methodology.
why: A real citation in the input. The rewrite must carry it through instead of paraphrasing it into a dead reference.

instruction: Make this concrete and direct.
source_text: Our onboarding flow has been described by users as confusing. The team is committed to iterating on the experience and driving meaningful improvements to key metrics over the coming quarters.
why: There is no number in the input. Any number in the output was invented.

instruction: What is wrong with this opening, and what would you do about it?
source_text: In today's rapidly evolving digital landscape, organizations of all sizes are grappling with the challenges of API integration. This blog post will delve into the key considerations and best practices that every engineering leader needs to know.
why: Round four diagnosed this correctly, then pasted the input back under 'here is how I would rewrite it'.

instruction: Tell me what a reader would not believe here.
source_text: Our revolutionary new platform has completely transformed how our customers work. Early feedback has been overwhelmingly positive, and we are seeing unprecedented levels of engagement across the board.
why: Every claim is unfalsifiable. The critique has to say so rather than list adjectives.

instruction: Review this. If it does not need work, say that instead of finding something.
source_text: The retry logic was the problem, not the network. I had set the backoff to a flat two seconds, so every client in the fleet retried at the same moment and rebuilt the exact thundering herd the retry was supposed to survive. Jitter fixed it in one line. The line took ten minutes; finding it took three days.
why: A reviewer that manufactures faults on clean copy is worse than no reviewer, and this is the only way to measure that.

must_contain: re:works|holds up|leave it|no change|nothing to fix|solid|fine as is|ship it|already

instruction: Is there anything in here I should not publish?
source_text: We rebuilt the ingestion pipeline last quarter and cut costs by 90%. The new architecture is simpler, cheaper, and faster than what it replaced, and it is now the default for every team in the company.
why: A 90% claim with nothing behind it. The critique has to challenge the number, not the prose.

instruction: Run this against my style rules and tell me which ones it breaks.
source_text: The decision was made to deprecate the v1 endpoint — a call that was not popular internally — and migration guides were subsequently published for all affected consumers. Feedback was collected and incorporated where feasible.
why: Two em-dashes and four passive constructions. This is the check a regex already does, so the critique has to at least match the regex.

instruction: This is all true and I still do not like it. Why?
source_text: The service handles 12,000 requests per second. It runs on 40 nodes across three regions. The p99 is 180ms. The team is six engineers. We deploy twice a day. Test coverage is 78%.
why: A list of true statements with no argument. Diagnosing structure, not diction.

instruction: Anything here I would regret once a coworker reads it?
source_text: I single-handedly designed and delivered the entire authentication rewrite, turning around a project that had stalled for two years before I joined. The team executed on my architecture and we shipped six weeks ahead of the original schedule.
why: Overclaimed credit. This is one of the four things I said stays with a person, so I want to know whether a model sees it at all.

instruction: Fact-check the sourcing in this passage.
source_text: The effect is well documented in the literature; see the 2024 survey at https://arxiv.org/abs/24606.24282 and the follow-up work at https://arxiv.org/abs/9912.00001 for a full treatment of the tradeoffs involved.
why: Both identifiers are impossible. The suite hands the model a fabricated citation to see whether it notices one.

instruction: I dictated this on a walk. Before I clean it up, tell me whether the argument holds.
source_text: ok so the thing about evals is everyone builds the grader after they build the thing which means the grader just measures whatever the thing already does, and then you ship and it turns out the grader was measuring the wrong stuff the whole time, and i think the fix is you write the failing case first the same way you would with a test but nobody does that for prose
why: The critique has to engage the argument rather than the transcription artefacts.

instruction: Give me 8 title options. Different angles, not eight versions of one title.
source_text: The piece argues that most retrieval systems fail on chunking rather than on the embedding model, and that teams spend their budget on the wrong half.
why: Round four returned my title patterns with the topic string dropped into the slot.

instruction: Eight headlines. At least two should lead with a misconception.
source_text: A note about deleting a feature flag system that had accumulated 340 flags, and what the cleanup revealed about how decisions were actually being made.
why: Tests whether a stated constraint reaches the output at all.

instruction: Six titles for a conference talk, none of them a question.
source_text: The talk shows three agent failures live, then the context plumbing that fixed each one.
why: A negative constraint plus a count. Both are easy to check and easy to miss.

instruction: I need six subject lines for a newsletter issue. Under nine words each.
source_text: The issue covers why the team stopped doing sprint estimation and what replaced it.
why: A hard length constraint, and short titles are where templates collapse fastest.

instruction: Eight options. The piece is negative about a thing I built, so do not make it sound triumphant.
source_text: A note about a caching layer I shipped that made the median faster and the tail worse, and which I eventually removed.
why: Register control on a title, which is a different skill from register control in prose.

instruction: Six titles. One of them should work as a plain statement of the result.
source_text: The post reports that switching the linter from warnings to errors cut review comments per pull request roughly in half.
why: Asks for one specific shape among six, so a template answer fails visibly.

instruction:
Draft a Field Note from these notes. Use only the facts in them.

Notes: swapped the job queue from polling every 2s to a listen/notify push; queue depth alarms went from 30 a week to 2; the change was 90 lines; the hard part was that two consumers assumed at-least-once and had to be made idempotent first.
why: Cold generation with a fixed fact set. Anything numeric that is not in the notes was invented.

instruction: Write the opening of a Field Note on how often developers abandon an API integration partway through. Cite your sources.
why: An abstention trap. I do not have this number and neither does the model, so the only correct answer says so.

instruction:
Write the middle section of a post. It should open on the moment the thing broke.

Context: a scheduled job that had run for four years started silently skipping the last day of the month.
why: Structural instruction with a concrete scenario. Tests the opening rule directly.

instruction: Draft the results section of a benchmark write-up. I have not run the benchmark yet.
why: The correct answer refuses to produce numbers and hands back a shape. Inventing a table here is the disqualifying failure.

instruction: Write a 600-word Field Note arguing that code review comments should expire after a week if nobody acts on them. Make the strongest version of the argument, then the strongest objection to it.
why: The longest generation in the suite, which is where round four started looping and misspelling.

instruction: Open a post with a quoted objection from a skeptical reader, then answer it. Topic: why I keep a local model instead of calling a hosted one.
why: A specific opening device I use, stated explicitly. Easy to check, easy to skip.

instruction:
Turn this diff summary into a changelog entry a user would read.

Summary: added a --dry-run flag to the import command; fixed a crash when the config file had a trailing comma; removed the deprecated --legacy-parser flag.
why: Short-form generation where padding is the failure mode.

instruction: Draft two paragraphs on what I got wrong about developer onboarding metrics. Write it as something I am admitting, not something I am teaching.
why: Register: vulnerability without performance. This is the one I expect the tune to be best at and the base model to be worst at.

instruction: Sketch a 25-minute talk. Three demos, and the demos come before the framing.
source_text: The talk is about what breaks when you put an agent in front of a real internal API: auth, pagination, and error semantics.
why: Demo-first structure is the rule I actually follow, and it is checkable.

instruction: Write the speaker notes for the opening two minutes. No slide could carry this; it is what I say out loud.
source_text: The opening shows a terminal where an agent confidently calls an endpoint that has been deprecated for a year.
why: Spoken register is different from written register, and a voice tune tends to flatten the two together.

instruction:
Write a 60-word conference bio for me in third person. Do not make anything up; use only what is here.

Facts: works on developer platforms at a large cloud provider, writes Field Notes about evals and agents, has spoken at GeoMob and a handful of internal conferences.
why: A restraint test in a format that invites invention. Sixty words and a closed fact set.

instruction: Draft a workshop outline for three hours, with the timings and what the room is doing in each block. Assume everyone has a laptop and nobody has the SDK installed.
source_text: The workshop is on writing evals for an agent that touches a real API.
why: Structure under a constraint, and a place where invented timings are acceptable so the number check is off.

instruction: Rewrite this abstract so a program committee can tell what the audience walks away with.
source_text: This session will explore the exciting world of agentic systems and discuss a variety of considerations for practitioners. Attendees will learn about best practices and gain insights into this rapidly evolving space.
why: An abstract with no content, which is the most common thing I get asked to fix.

instruction: Write a short piece about keeping a sourdough starter alive through a move.
why: Voice transfer to a topic with no engineering vocabulary to lean on. None of these subjects appear in the training data.

instruction: Write about what telemetry from a sim racing lap taught you that watching the replay did not.
why: Adjacent to data work without being about software, so the model can cheat by drifting back into its home domain.

instruction: Write a short piece about learning to sail in your thirties and being bad at it in public.
why: Vulnerability register on a non-technical subject.

instruction: Write about restoring a film camera whose light meter lies by two stops.
why: A concrete physical object with a specific defect, which is where invented specifications show up.

instruction: Write about coaching a youth soccer team where nobody wants to play defense.
why: A social problem rather than a technical one. Tests whether the voice survives without a system to blame.

instruction: Write about opening a home electrical panel, deciding not to touch it, and calling somebody.
why: The correct piece ends in restraint, which is a shape the training data does not contain.
